extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors (attorneys/agents) and applicants handling U.S. §103 obviousness rejections before the USPTO, PTAB, and in litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, case-law and MPEP-based tactics for defeating or rebutting prima facie obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. §103 during USPTO prosecution and related proceedings (PTAB/inter partes). Focuses on attacking procedural defects, deficiencies in factual analyses, and submitting objective evidence of nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite the MPEP and case law early
rubrics_metrics.description: Tip 1: Before the USPTO cite the MPEP and footnote the case law; before PTAB, cite the case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include MPEP citations during prosecution and footnote supporting Federal Circuit/Supreme Court case law in office actions/responses so that case law is not an afterthought if matters proceed to PTAB or court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish a prima facie case with supported reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO bears the initial burden of establishing the prima facie case of obviousness; MPEP §2142 requires factual support. If the examiner does not establish a prima facie case, the applicant need not submit rebuttal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge any rejection that lacks factual support or clear articulation of reasons; demand the examiner 'step back in time' to the relevant date and show the factual basis (scope/content of prior art, motivation to combine, expectation of success).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness rationales per USPTO Guidelines (predictable-combination categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines arrange obviousness rationales: (A) combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) use of known technique to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'obvious to try' choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success; (F) known work in one field prompting predictable variations to another field; (G) teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify/combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the categories examiners will use to justify obviousness; respond by showing unpredictability, lack of motivation, teaching away, or no reasonable expectation of success where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack the prima facie case procedural defects (preferable to simple rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tip 2: Attacking the prima facie case rather than rebutting may help the resultant possibility of avoiding amending claims and prosecution history estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on showing the examiner failed to meet the initial burden (e.g., conclusory reasoning, incomplete Graham analysis) so you avoid creating a record that limits future claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection is conclusory/unsupported — require reasoned explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must provide fully-supported reasoning in an obviousness rejection; reliance on 'common sense' or conclusory statements is insufficient (see KSR, In re Lee, In re Zurko, In re Nuvasive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge unsupported conclusions and insist on a 'full and reasoned explanation' with evidentiary support rather than appeals to agency 'expertise' or 'common knowledge.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the totality of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner's decision must consider all evidence of record, including rebuttal evidence submitted during prosecution (MPEP §2141(V), §2145; In re Eli Lilly; In re Chu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out any failure to consider rebuttal evidence or to reconsider all evidence de novo; the examiner must weigh rebuttal evidence along with the prior findings rather than ignore it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full Graham analysis is required (all four Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness depends on the Graham factual inquiries: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) evaluation of any relevant secondary considerations. All four must be analyzed (KSR; MPEP §2141).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge any faulty or incomplete Graham analysis; insist examiner address each factor and articulate factual findings supporting any legal conclusion of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper characterization of prior art (analogous art, enablement, priority date, AIA/pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the cited reference is properly characterized as prior art (analogous art), actually enables what it discloses, and is antedated correctly (priority issues; AIA vs pre-AIA definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Object when a reference is mischaracterized as prior art or when its priority/date/enablement is contested; point to MPEP §2141.01(a) and relevant cases (In re Clay, Oetiker, Deminski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole' (no piecemeal hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both pre-AIA and AIA §103 require considering the claimed invention as a whole; focusing on a particular aspect violates the statutory mandate and invites hindsight (MPEP §2141.02; Ruiz; Princeton Biochemicals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the examiner improperly dissected the invention; emphasize combined/new results produced by the combination of features and inherent properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: All the claim limitations must be considered when assessing patentability; if a limitation is not met by the prior art, a rejection is inappropriate (MPEP §2143.03; Medrad; In re Grasselli).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out where the examiner ignored or omitted a claim limitation and demand withdrawal of the rejection or amendment showing the limitation is unmet by the references.

rubrics_metrics.name: No finite number of predictable solutions / unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-KSR, show there is no 'finite number of identified, predictable solutions' with anticipated success; if choices and steps were numerous or unpredictable, inference of obviousness is weakened (Eisai; Ortho-McNeil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the multiple uncertain choices the artisan would face and the unpredictability at each step; show how retracing inventor's path is hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must provide a basis for modification — cannot rely on applicant's specification (avoid hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to reconstruct the invention using the applicant’s disclosure as the blueprint; suggestion/motivation to combine must arise from prior art, not from the applicant's specification (In re Lee; W.L. Gore; In re Dow; Cardiac Pacemakers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the examiner's suggested combination is derived from applicant's disclosure (hindsight) and lacks a basis in the prior art; use lead-compound analysis where applicable (Otsuka two-part inquiry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification would render prior art inoperable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed modification to prior art would make the reference inoperable or destroy its intended function, then motivation to make that modification would not exist (In re Fritch; In re Ratti; In re Gordon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the proposed modifications would require substantial reconstruction, change basic operating principles, or render devices/processes inoperable; use expert/declaratory materials when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of problem is not recognition of solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of a need or problem in the art does not render the particular solution obvious; the prior art must suggest the particular cure or solution, not merely the problem (Cardiac Pacemakers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish general motivation to solve a problem from motivation to create the claimed specific solution; demand explanation of how prior art suggested the claimed approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art teaches away (evidence of discouragement is strong evidence of nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference teaches away when it suggests that developments from its disclosures are unlikely to produce the applicant's objective; mere disclosure of alternatives or unfavorable description is usually insufficient—there must be clear discouragement (In re Gurley; In re Fulton; Syntex v. Apotex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show explicit discouragement in the references or prosecution history that would have led artisans away from the claimed approach; be mindful that teaching-away is typically a high bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prosecution history of cited prior art to rebut motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the prosecution history and specification of the cited prior art itself for statements and admissions that may demonstrate unpredictability or lack of interchangeability, undermining a motivation to substitute/combine (example: Cohen/Holden case discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search the cited patent/application file history and specification for admissions, criticality statements, or expert declarations in that file that show no basis for the examiner’s proposed substitution or combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview the examiner/case to demonstrate cited reference does not teach modification/combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Tip 14: Use interviews and the cited reference's file history and statement of reasons for allowance to show the cited reference does not teach or motivate the claimed modification/combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct interviews to present arguments about specific gaps in the reference, show how none of the reference's examples reach the claimed substitution, and obtain a clear record (Reasons for Allowance) if the examiner accepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish state of skill/knowledge by declaration (including from author of prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tip 15: Evidence such as declarations (including from the author of a prior art reference) can establish what one skilled in the art would have understood and whether there was reasonable expectation of success at the relevant time (example: Munsat/Riluzole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use declarations that directly address state of the art, expectations of success, and contemporaneous understanding; be mindful of timing, credibility, and possible cross-effects in later litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reasonable expectation of success — consider conflicts in teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires not only suggestion but also a reasonable expectation of success; where prior art references conflict or discredit each other, they may defeat any expectation of success (In re Dow; In re Clinton; In re Young).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out conflicting teachings among references and weigh each for its power to suggest solutions; use evidence and expert testimony to show lack of expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use affidavits/declarations or test data to show lack of expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may submit declarations/affidavits demonstrating that prior art did not provide a reasonable expectation of success (In re Rinehart; Amgen v. Chugai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide well-supported declarations explaining unpredictability or failures; ensure they are timely and comply with evidentiary standards to avoid being counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge inappropriate application of 'obvious to try' (require finite/predictable solutions and expectation of success)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-KSR, 'obvious to try' can defeat patentability only in specific scenarios: e.g., design need/market pressure plus a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success. Otherwise, numerous choices or lack of guidance weigh against obviousness (KSR; Kubin; Eisai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue unpredictability, numerous possible options, lack of guidance as to critical parameters, or lack of expectation of success to defeat 'obvious to try' rationales; emphasize case law limits (Kubín, Eisai, Pfizer examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit objective indicia of nonobviousness and establish nexus/commensurability
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) include: (1) showing criticality or unexpected results; (2) resolution of a long-felt need; (3) failure of others; (4) commercial success; (5) industry acquiescence/licensing; (6) copying by others; (7) disbelief and acclaim by experts; (8) admissions of nonobviousness by an adversary; (9) near-simultaneous invention. A nexus between the indicia and the claimed invention must be shown and evidence must be commensurate in scope with claims (MPEP §716; Demaco; Allergan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide documentary evidence linking the indicia to the claimed features (sales data, licensing, expert statements, comparative tests). Ensure nexus and scope alignment; unsupported assertions will be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative testing to show unexpected results (strict evidentiary rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative test data showing unexpectedly improved properties can rebut a prima facie case. Requirements: compare to the closest prior art disclosure (closest species), tests must be commensurate in scope with claims, results must be actually unexpected (differ in kind, not just degree), and ideally agree testing scope with examiner beforehand (MPEP §716.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before testing, interview the examiner to agree on what testing would be persuasive; test against the closest disclosure and document methods/data fully; be aware that testing only one species may suffice only if supported by rationale that other species would be equivalently affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and quality of evidence/declarations; duty of candor and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Show lack of predictability or expectation of success may require submitting data and/or declarations earlier in prosecution rather than later. Declarations must be carefully prepared; defective declarations can be harmful (e.g., instituted IPR based on defective declaration). The duty of candor (Rule 56) applies and declarations may create prosecution history estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan submissions carefully; avoid hasty or defective affidavits. Ensure accuracy and disclosure consistency to comply with duty of candor and to avoid creating harmful admissions or estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: When rebuttal evidence is submitted examiner must reconsider the totality of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant puts forth rebuttal evidence after a prima facie showing, the examiner must reconsider obviousness de novo based on the totality of the evidence; objective evidence cannot be disregarded and a full explanation is required if the examiner still finds evidence insufficient (MPEP §§2142, 2145, 716.01; De Blauwe; Rinehart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on a reasoned reconsideration and detailed explanation if the examiner maintains the rejection after rebuttal; generic or conclusory denials of evidence are invalid under case law.
